segments.t: Along a Sapporo riverbank, Toshi and Toru Muranishi spot a cheerful older stranger named Ikezawa. After musing aloud that people naturally crave whatever stays hidden, Ikezawa walks straight up to Muranishi and invites him along. Listen to how Toshi's blunt street suspicions contrast with Ikezawa's easy charm and Muranishi's calm poise.
何だ、あいつ。
ほらほら、もう少しだよ。
でもな、隠れてるからこそ見たくなるもんだろ？
違うか？
まあ、頑張ってな。
よう、あんただろ？
北海道の会長の村西さんってのは。
そうです。
ちょっとつきあってくれないかな？
ちょっと。
あんた、誰？
いいですよ、おつきあいしましょう。
Watch how one request shifts from Ikezawa's casual invitation to Muranishi's polished reply. Let's take the key lines apart.
何だ、あいつ。

'Who is that guy?' Toshi blurts out "nan da", literally 'what is it?', before pointing at the stranger as "aitsu". Save "aitsu" for rough, gossipy talk—polite speech uses "ano hito", that person, instead.
ほらほら、もう少しだよ。
'Come on, just a little more.' Doubling "hora" into "horahora" works like a playful 'look, come on now'. After it, "mou sukoshi" combines "mou", a bit further, with "sukoshi", a little.
でもな、隠れてるからこそ見たくなるもんだろ？

'Still, precisely because something is hidden, you want to see it, right?' Putting "kara koso" onto "kakureteru", is hidden, sharpens 'because' into 'for that very reason'. Then "mitaku naru" links "mitai", want to see, with "naru", become.
違うか？
'Am I wrong?' Two syllables plus a question tag—"chigau ka" comes from "chigau", to differ or be wrong. In everyday conversation, "chigau" on its own is the quickest way to say 'no, that is not it'.
まあ、頑張ってな。
'Well, keep at it.' Starting with "maa" softens the parting remark like English 'well then'. "Ganbatte" comes from "ganbaru", to hang in there and do your best, warmed up at the end by friendly "na".
よう、あんただろ？
'Hey, it is you, right?' "You" is a breezy masculine 'hey', and "anta" trims standard "anata" down to a familiar, slightly bossy 'you'. Ending with "daro" guesses aloud and expects a nod back.
北海道の会長の村西さんってのは。

'Chairman Muranishi of Hokkaido.' "Kaichou" means board chairman, built from "kai", association or company, and "chou", head. At the tail, "tte no wa" wraps the whole title up as 'the one people call'.
そうです。
'That is right.' Calm and crisp, "sou desu" pairs "sou", so or that way, with polite "desu" to confirm a fact in two words.
ちょっとつきあってくれないかな？

'Would you come along with me for a bit?' "Chotto" literally means a little, softening the favor right away. "Tsukiatte" comes from "tsukiau", to keep someone company, and "kurenai kana" asks 'would you not do this for me, I wonder?'
あんた、誰？
'Who are you?' Toshi throws "anta" right back and adds "dare", the core question word for 'who', skipping any polite ending altogether.
いいですよ、おつきあいしましょう。

'Sure, I will join you.' Opening with "ii desu yo" gives an easy 'sure, fine by me'. Notice how Muranishi dresses Ikezawa's plain "tsukiau" in respectful "o-tsukiai shimashou", turning 'tag along' into 'let me accompany you'. Now let's listen to the whole riverbank encounter again from start to finish.
何だ、あいつ。
ほらほら、もう少しだよ。
でもな、隠れてるからこそ見たくなるもんだろ？
違うか？
まあ、頑張ってな。
よう、あんただろ？
北海道の会長の村西さんってのは。
そうです。
ちょっとつきあってくれないかな？
ちょっと。
あんた、誰？
いいですよ、おつきあいしましょう。

Did you catch the mirror between "tsukiatte kurenai kana" and "o-tsukiai shimashou"? The same root "tsukiau", keeping someone company, shifts from street-level warmth to business polish just by adding "o" at the front and "shimashou" at the end. Until next time, see you soon.
また会いましょう。
